title: "research"

My research is broadly about **complex systems and nonlinear dynamics**.

A question that keeps showing up in what I do is deceptively simple:

> **How does structure shape dynamics?**

In networked systems, the way components interact can strongly constrain the collective behaviors that emerge. During my PhD, I've been exploring this question in the context of **higher-order networks**, with a particular interest in **symmetry and synchronization**.

## higher-order networks

Traditional networks represent interactions as links between pairs of nodes. This is an incredibly useful abstraction, but not every interaction is naturally pairwise.

In many systems, interactions can involve three or more components simultaneously. **Higher-order networks** provide a framework for representing these interactions explicitly, using structures such as hypergraphs and simplicial complexes.

A large part of my work involves understanding what changes — structurally and dynamically — when we move from ordinary graphs to these higher-order representations.

## symmetry

Symmetry provides a way of identifying parts of a network that are structurally equivalent.

For ordinary graphs, these symmetries can be described through graph automorphisms. In higher-order networks, things become more interesting: there are different ways of representing the same system, and the relationship between the symmetries of these representations is not always obvious.

I'm interested in understanding these symmetries, how they can be detected, and what they can tell us about the dynamics supported by the network.

## cluster synchronization

Synchronization doesn't necessarily mean that every node in a system behaves identically.

Instead, subsets of nodes can synchronize with each other while remaining dynamically distinct from the rest of the network. This phenomenon is known as **cluster synchronization**.

One of the main questions I'm exploring is how these synchronized clusters relate to the structural symmetries of higher-order networks — including when symmetry predicts possible synchronization patterns and, perhaps more interestingly, when it doesn't.

## beyond symmetry

Structure can tell us a lot about dynamics, but perhaps not everything.

Part of my current work is concerned with situations in which synchronized patterns cannot be explained by conventional automorphisms alone. This raises a broader question that I find particularly interesting:

> **How much can we actually infer about dynamics from structure alone?**

Answering that requires looking beyond conventional symmetry descriptions and exploring more general ways of relating network structure to dynamically invariant patterns.
